items.body: After two self-released albums, Bagger 258 have a label. “Der Technokrat”, a two-track digital single, came out on August 28, 2026 through Scanner, the Dark Dimensions imprint that also handles The Saint Paul, Resistor and Akalotz. The Augsburg EBM duo of Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim Schmelzer pair the original (3:31) with “Der Technokrat (The Saint Paul Edit)” (3:45), reworked by label-mate The Saint Paul. The single is available to stream and download on Bandcamp, where it sits in the Scanner catalogue alongside the label’s other 2026 releases, and on the usual streaming services. There is no physical edition. Der Technokrat by Bagger 258 What ‘Der Technokrat’ is about The band describe the song as a story in two halves: an authority that demands obedience, then a workforce that stops obeying. In the label notes they write that the track “explores the conflict between totalitarian control and individual resistance within an industrialized system” and that “the initial oppression gives way to open revolt: the working class refuses to comply, dismantles the existing power structures, and confronts the corrupt leadership with a collective claim to self-determination.” The theme continues the factory-floor vocabulary that runs through the Bagger 258 catalogue, from the albums “Ode an die Arbeit” and “Aufwärts gehts bergab”, where track titles include “Arbeiterwut”, “Werkshalle 4” and “Schicht im Schacht”. Musically the duo stay with the stripped-down, bassline-led EBM they have used since their debut. The label notes describe the track as built on “a relentless, machine-driven foundation of pounding beats, forceful basslines, and a dark, high-energy atmosphere”. “Der Technokrat” is the first new Bagger 258 material since the second album “Aufwärts gehts bergab”, released on February 20, 2026, and the first Bagger 258 release to appear on Scanner. The duo had already remixed for the label: their version of “The Undertaker” by Gamma Vortex came out through Scanner in September 2025. About Bagger 258 Bagger 258 formed in Augsburg, Germany as the EBM duo of Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim Schmelzer, both also members of Projekt 26. They set out to revive the direct, bass-driven style associated with Anhalt EBM. In a Side-Line interview Schmelzer said they “were on a mission to resurrect something no one seemed to be messing with anymore – that punchy, in-your-face Anhalt EBM”. Von der Eisenmühle summed up the Bagger 258 method in the same conversation: “we’re after basslines that make you stomp, a brutal vibe, and tunes that stick with you.” The self-released debut album “Ode an die Arbeit” came out on November 24, 2023, mixed by Daniel Hallhuber of Young & Cold Records in Augsburg and mastered by Stefan Poiss of Mind.In.A.Box, and reached first place in the Deutsche Alternative Charts. Side-Line reviewed it in February 2024 and interviewed the duo the following month. Two digital singles followed in 2024: “Körperkommando” on June 21, with remixes by Kreign, Tension Control and Gamma Vortex, and “Alter Mann” on November 19. Both title tracks were carried over to the second album. “Aufwärts gehts bergab” arrived on February 20, 2026 as a digital release and a CD digipak limited to 258 copies, mixed and mastered by Krischan Jan-Eric Wesenberg at Studio 600 in Gelsenkirchen, Its thirteen tracks run “Arbeiterwut”, “Alter Mann”, “Funktion, Kontrolle!”, “Werkshalle 4”, “Erzengel”, “Körperkommando”, “Exakt!”, “Body 258”, “…und der Rest ist Geschichte” and “Schicht im Schacht”, closed by remixes of “Werkshalle 4” by Nachtmahr, of “…und der Rest ist Geschichte” by NordarR and of “Body 258” by Menticide. The duo play Nocturnal Culture Night 19 in Deutzen on the weekend of September 4-6, 2026. Both albums and the 2024 singles remain available through the band’s own Bandcamp page, separate from the Scanner catalogue that hosts the new single. “Der Technokrat” moves the project from self-release to the Scanner / Dark Dimensions roster.

items.body: Cicero, the Scottish synthpop artist whom Pet Shop Boys signed to their Spaghetti Recordings label in the early 1990s, has remixed Danish synthpop duo SoftWave. “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)” comes out on 18 September 2026 as a self-released digital single, mastered by Nordic Music Group, with cover artwork by Jason Stetson. A pre-save link is live. The remix returns a favour. SoftWave’s friend and collaborator Barney Ashton-Bullock, working for Cherry Red, introduced the duo to Cicero, and SoftWave went on to remix his 1992 single “Love Is Everywhere”, a track produced by Pet Shop Boys with Neil Tennant on backing vocals. Their version appeared on 29 September 2023 on the 3CD 30th anniversary expanded edition of Cicero’s album “Future Boy”, where it sits on the “Ciceroddities!” disc next to four other new remixes of the song and live recordings from Heaven in 1991. Three years later Cicero takes the controls for SoftWave. The duo describe his version as one that “brings a distinctive retro synthpop and Italo-disco flavour to the track, while preserving the melody and emotional core of the original.” “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)” is the second of three singles leading up to “things we’ve remixed”, SoftWave’s remix album due on 23 October 2026. The first was “Supernova (Aspra Remix)”, released on 21 August 2026 and made by Aspra, the solo project of Marsheaux’s Sophia Sarigiannidou. The album collects nine remixes by producers from six countries and marks more than a decade of the duo’s collaborations. From ‘Aspire’ to ‘things we’ve remixed’: the history of ‘Wake Up’ The original “Wake Up” first appeared on the five-track EP “Aspire”, released digitally on 14 October 2022 and reviewed on Side-Line as “Aspire”. SoftWave described it at the time as the song for people who cannot get out of bed early. A year later the track was carried over to the album “things we’ve done”, out digitally on 13 October 2023, on CD through Electro-Shock Records on 20 October 2023 and on vinyl on 21 June 2024. Jerry Olsen wrote the music and played the synthesizers, Catrine Christensen sang and wrote the lyrics, and Nordic Music Group’s Jacob Cederberg mixed and mastered the album. A remix compilation after every release has become a habit for the duo. “Together Alone The Remixes” (2017) followed the debut EP with nine remixes from six countries, and “Game On 1Up” (2019) reworked the debut album with twelve remixers, among them former Human League member Ian Burden. “things we’ve remixed” is the third such collection. About SoftWave SoftWave formed in Denmark in 2014 as the duo of Catrine Christensen (vocals, lyrics) and Jerry Olsen (synthesizers, production), working out of their own Blue Orange Studio. They mix classic British-styled synthpop with dance-pop and name Erasure as an inspiration. The debut EP “Together Alone” came out on 27 May 2016, followed by “Together Alone The Remixes” on 15 February 2017 and a remake of “Everything Change” for the Danish Electro Vol. 01 compilation in February 2018. The debut album “Game On” arrived in April 2019 on digital, LP and CD, preceded by the singles “Something Is Missing”, “No Need To Hide” and “Galaxy Of Stars”; Side-Line reviewed the vinyl edition of “Game On”. The remix album “Game On 1Up” followed on 19 November 2019 and was reissued on CD by Electro-Shock Records on 1 October 2020 with a live bonus track recorded at Rockefeller in Oslo, where SoftWave supported OMD on the Scandinavian leg of the “Souvenir” tour in February 2020 (Side-Line review: “Game On 1Up”). In 2021 the duo produced two remixes for Andy Bell‘s “Club Torsten!” LP on Cherry Red, and on 11 June 2021 they released the single “System Failure”. The EP “Aspire” (14 October 2022) was followed by the Christmas single “Will It Ever Be Christmas Again” on 1 December 2022, co-written with Barney Ashton-Bullock, and by the second album “things we’ve done” in October 2023. That same autumn SoftWave’s remix of “Love Is Everywhere” appeared on Cicero’s “Future Boy” expanded edition. A 12″ vinyl EP of the Christmas single, with a radio edit, an interview and a new remix, came out on 24 November 2025. The remix album “things we’ve remixed”, opened by “Supernova (Aspra Remix)” in August 2026 and continued by “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)” on 18 September, is due on 23 October 2026.

items.body: Sardinian dark disco and coldwave producer Matrukk released “Diavoleide” on Cat Cave Records on 28 August 2026. The digital single carries two takes on the same track, a long version and a short version, and is out on Bandcamp. Matteo Girometti, who records as Matrukk, produced the release and handled the additional mix, and is credited as executive producer. Valeria Black Val took the cover photograph, with Michele Manca as model and the shoot located at the Follesa house in Donori, Sardinia. Girometti did the cover graphics and post-production himself. Diavoleide by Matrukk What ‘Diavoleide’ follows in the Matrukk catalogue The single is the producer’s second Cat Cave Records release of 2026. It follows “In the Shadow of Neon Light”, issued on 22 May 2026, which Girometti composed and produced alone, with mastering by Matteo “Mr Bizz” Floris and cover photography again by Valeria Black Val. Before that came “Scary Female (Sbikka Dark Tech Groove Revibe)” on 10 April 2026, a rework of a track from his own catalogue. Both versions of “Diavoleide” run on the same material, with the long version giving the arrangement more room and the short version cut for shorter play. About Matrukk Matrukk is the recording name of Matteo Girometti, a producer and DJ born in Cagliari, Sardinia. He worked for the Rome record shop Goody Music before turning to production, and his releases mix dark disco, coldwave, darkwave and dark electronic material. His first release under the name, the two-track “Witches Screaming ep”, came out on 11 May 2025 and paired “Witches Screaming”, featuring Katarina Rose and f r a g i l e, with “Creepy Girl”, featuring Alesia Davina. Matteo “Mr Bizz” Floris mastered both tracks. The “Dark Night ep” followed on 5 October 2025 with “Dark Night”, featuring Katarina Rose, Sample_me and Dzerit, and a second version of “Scary Female” with Alesia Davina. Sbikka’s rework of “Scary Female” arrived in April 2026, and “In the Shadow of Neon Light” in May. “Diavoleide” is his fifth release in sixteen months and his second single of 2026. No album has been announced.

items.body: Three new tracks in thirteen minutes: that is the whole of “Melting Point X1”, the digital EP that Chainreactor released on August 28, 2026 through ProNoize, the Dark Dimensions imprint that has carried the project since 2009. The Düsseldorf industrial techno project of Jens Minor pairs the EP with an official video for the opening track, “Permagna”, which went up on the label’s YouTube channel the same day. The EP consists of “Permagna” (4:52), “Maybe, Maybe not” (4:30) and “S!ck Mode” (3:35). It is a digital-only release, available to stream and download on Bandcamp, where it is also part of the ProNoize label discography. Melting Point X1 by Chainreactor ‘Permagna’ and the sound of ‘Melting Point X1’ ProNoize presents the EP as a return to the project’s first records. The label text calls the three cuts “raw, hard-hitting, and unapologetically dirty” and says the EP “embraces the project’s original DNA: no gimmicks, no compromises”. Chainreactor has built its tracks on samples rather than sung vocals since “Interlinked” in 2020, after a period with Kay Schäfer as singer, and the label text places the new EP in that line. Side-Line has reviewed each of the last five Chainreactor albums and EPs, from “Interlinked” in 2020 to “War Machinery” in 2025. “Melting Point X1” is the second Chainreactor release of 2026 after the one-track digital single “Unintentional Presence – Part 2” on April 24, and the first EP since “The Essence” in 2021. It also continues a direction Side-Line noted on the last album: the “War Machinery” review described Minor as circling “back to his roots – delivering raw power through a perfect fusion of Dark-Electro, Industrial, and Rave”, with spoken-word samples in place of vocals. That twelve-track album, which includes “No Apologies”, “Roar”, “Go”, “Kalt” and “Unendlichkeit”, was the tenth in the Chainreactor catalogue. ProNoize is the harder electronic arm of Dark Dimensions, the German label group that also runs Scanner, and it has released every Chainreactor album since the 2009 debut. Its Bandcamp catalogue now lists 86 releases, and the new EP is sold there as a single digital download rather than as part of a physical edition. About Chainreactor Chainreactor started in 2009 as the solo project of German producer Jens Minor. The debut album “X-Tinction” came out on ProNoize the same year, followed by “Insomniac” (2011), “The Silence & The Noise” (2013), “Mass Driver” (2014), “Dirt” (2015) and “Decayed Values” (2017), all on the same label. Kay Schäfer joined as a second member and singer during that stretch, and a “Rare Stuff & Remixes” compilation collected loose tracks in 2017. Minor mixes hard techno, power noise, EBM and trance elements into a club-oriented industrial sound that he has called “a testing range where I can put all the influences of music that I like to something new” in a Side-Line interview. The seventh album, “Interlinked” (2020), dropped vocals again in favour of samples, a decision Schäfer, who had become a full member and the singer on the preceding albums, explained in that interview: “Chainreactor is about creating a certain atmosphere and feeling and this is done through the music itself and not through lyrics.” Videos for “Interlinked”, “Grey” and “The Wicked” accompanied that twelve-track album. The EP “The Essence” followed in 2021, then the albums “Techno Body Device” (2022), “Venom” (2023) and, as a solo project once more, “War Machinery” (2025), the tenth Chainreactor album. The digital singles “Welcome To The Deep” (four tracks) and “Destroyer Of Worlds” (two tracks) followed in 2024, then “Roar” and “30 Ghosts 2K25” in 2025, all of them on ProNoize. “Melting Point X1” follows “War Machinery” by a year and returns to the format of the project’s early, sample-driven records.

items.album: djrum mixes the next ‘DJ-Kicks’ for !K7, with four new tracks and exclusives by Skee Mask and Clark

items.body: !K7 Records has handed its next DJ-Kicks mix to djrum. “DJ-Kicks: djrum” arrives on 16 October 2026 as a signed 2LP EcoRecord, a standard 2LP EcoRecord, a digipak CD and a digital album, and is available to pre-order. The London DJ and producer Felix Manuel mixed it live from vinyl on three turntables, then chopped, collaged and overdubbed the result in the studio. The mix carries four new djrum productions – “Turning”, “Psychic Video”, “Leave Me Alone” and “To Do What To Do” – alongside exclusive tracks by Skee Mask and Clark. “Psychic Video” is the lead single and is out now. DJ-Kicks: djrum by djrum The mix moves through ambient, classical, post-punk, acid, breakcore and percussive minimalism, and it runs on a thread of field recordings by Chris Watson, the sound recordist who co-founded Cabaret Voltaire in Sheffield in 1973 and left the group in 1981 to record for television. Three Watson pieces sit in the mix: “Glastonbury Ocean Soundscape” opens it, “El Divisadero” runs past the halfway mark and “Waiting (aka Adult Cheetah)” closes side D on vinyl. Between them djrum places Venetian Snares, The Raincoats, emptyset, upsammy, Bugge Wesseltoft and E Wata. “I like things to be a bit bumpy,” djrum said of the sequencing, “to have ups and downs and fck with expectations!”* Manuel described his studio process as “meditational”, and he named DJ Food, “who, I think, is my most revered DJ of all time”, as an influence on the record. The press release describes the single “Psychic Video” as “a convulsive, percussive-heavy roller of mind-bending electronics with chopped spoken word samples”. djrum’s ‘DJ-Kicks’ tracklist The vinyl edition runs 14 tracks across four sides: A1. djrum – “Turning” A2. Skee Mask – “Flip” A3. |||||||||||||||||||| – “Causalities” A4. djrum – “Psychic Video” B1. djrum – “Leave Me Alone” B2. E Wata – “U D S2S” B3. Chewlie – “Run” C1. Bugge Wesseltoft – “Flimmer” C2. The Raincoats – “Only Loved At Night” C3. Clark – “Clonk Dual” C4. djrum – “To Do What To Do” D1. Chris Watson – “Waiting (aka Adult Cheetah)” D2. Lino Capra Vaccina – “Antico Adagio” D3. Chris Watson – “El Divisadero” The CD, streaming and continuous-mix edition runs 33 tracks, adding a reprise of the opening Chris Watson piece and Susumu Yokota’s “Fearful Dream”: Chris Watson – “Glastonbury Ocean Soundscape” djrum – “Turning” Venetian Snares – “Miss Balaton” Uwalmassa – “Untitled 12” Clark – “Clonk Dual” Human Resources – “New T” djrum – “Psychic Video” Idris Ackamoor & The Pyramids – “Traponga” Atrice – “Hatara” Lino Capra Vaccina – “Antico Adagio” Susumu Yokota – “Fearful Dream” Lo.Sai – “Voi Siete Qui” Kimyan Law – “Chungwa” Core Self – “Suspiria” The Raincoats – “Only Loved At Night” Chris Watson – “Glastonbury Ocean Soundscape (Reprise)” djrum – “Leave Me Alone” Chewlie – “Run” Bugge Wesseltoft – “Flimmer” Chris Watson – “El Divisadero” emptyset – “Point” Planet Battagon – “Salacians Of Trans-Neptunia” Skee Mask – “Flip” Eli Keszler – “Sun” E Wata – “U D S2S” Chris Watson – “Waiting (aka Adult Cheetah)” |||||||||||||||||||| – “Causalities” Mark – “Incantation For The Protection Of JC” upsammy – “Relict” A.Fruit – “Measures of Dispersion” Sandro Mussida – “EEE” djrum – “To Do What To Do” Actual Proof – “Maybe We’ll Stay (Sileni Remix)” The unmixed download edition holds 31 tracks, the same running order minus the Chris Watson reprise and the Susumu Yokota track. The DJ-Kicks series began in 1995 with C.J. Bolland’s volume and has run on !K7 since, with Modeselektor and Eris Drew delivering the last two entries of 2025. djrum’s edition is the third of 2026, after those by Sofia Kourtesis and TEED. djrum live dates 2026 djrum has played Lowlands, Gare in Porto and Gravitate Festival over the past two weeks. The remaining dates run into the new year: 22 August – Lowlands Festival, Biddinghuizen, NL (played) 29 August – Gare, Porto, PT (played) 30 August – Gravitate Festival, Alandroal, PT (played) 4 September – Draaimolen Festival, Tilburg, NL 11 September – Tresor / Globus, Berlin, DE 13 September – Waterworks Festival, London, UK 23 October – Zeezout, Amsterdam, NL 23 October – Club Raum ADE, Amsterdam, NL 24 October – Open Ground, Wuppertal, DE 28 November – KANAL, Brussels, BE 4 December – Cialo, Wrocław, PL 1 January 2027 – RADION, Amsterdam, NL About djrum djrum is the project of Felix Manuel, a London DJ and producer who learned piano at seven, trained as a jazz pianist and started DJing after inheriting his mother’s jazz record collection. He began by playing bass music, ragga and jungle at London squat parties and hosted a monthly show on Sub.FM. His first records, the “Mountains” EP (2011) and a second EP, came out on 2nd Drop, the label that released his debut album “Seven Lies” in 2013. A trilogy of EPs and the singles “LA” and “Space Race” followed in 2015 and 2016, before he signed to R&S Records for the “Broken Glass Arch” EP in November 2017 and the second album “Portrait With Firewood” in 2018, on which cellist Zosia Jagodzinska joined his own piano improvisations. The 2019 double A-side “Hard To Say” / “Tournesol” on R&S carried his own term for the material, “ambient-gabber”. After a five-year gap he moved to Houndstooth, the Fabric-affiliated label, for the “Meaning’s Edge” EP in late 2024, which reached number 15 on the UK albums chart, and the third album “Under Tangled Silence” on 25 April 2025, which peaked at number 9 on the UK albums chart and topped the dance albums chart. He supported it with a 32-date tour including Fabric in London and Primavera Sound. The “I Wander” EP, a 16-minute composition presented as one continuous track on vinyl and as seven edits digitally, followed on Houndstooth on 14 August 2026. As a DJ he mixes from vinyl on three turntables, moving between dubstep, drum and bass, breakcore, techno, trip-hop, jazz and ambient within one set, and it is that set-building method that “DJ-Kicks: djrum” documents on record for !K7.

items.body: Twelve days after the first live single, Till Lindemann has put out a second. “Du hast kein Herz (Live In Kraków)” appeared on streaming platforms on September 2, 2026, together with a live video cut from the concert footage. It follows “Übers Meer (Live In Kraków)”, which arrived on August 21, and both tracks preview “Live In Kraków”, the concert album and film that Out Of Line releases on September 25, 2026. The recording comes from the TAURON Arena in Kraków on December 1, 2025, one of the closing arena dates of the “Meine Welt” tour, and the video was published on the Till Lindemann YouTube channel. “Du hast kein Herz” sits fourteenth in the nineteen-track running order of the audio editions, three positions before “Übers Meer”. The show was filmed with twenty 4K cameras, six GoPros, two 360-degree rigs and a drone, and the live album is available in DTS-HD Master Audio 5.1 and 7.1 and Dolby Atmos alongside the stereo mix. Where ‘Du hast kein Herz’ comes from The studio version of “Du hast kein Herz” is the fifth track on “Zunge”, the album Lindemann released himself on November 3, 2023 after suspending a planned Universal Music release. Lindemann wrote the lyrics and Sky van Hoff wrote and produced the music. “Übers Meer”, the first live single, comes from the same album, where it sits one track earlier. Till Lindemann reissued that album in 2025 as “Zunge 2025”, adding nine tracks, three of them previously unreleased, plus remixes. The two Till Lindemann live singles so far draw only on “Zunge” material; the Kraków set also includes songs from the Lindemann duo albums (“Skills in Pills”, “Fat”, “Praise Abort”, “Fish On”, “Golden Shower”, “Knebel”, “Allesfresser”, “Blut”, “Platz 1”), the 2021 single “Ich hasse Kinder” and “Und die Engel singen” from the “Meine Welt” EP. The “Meine Welt” tour ran through arenas in seventeen countries from late October 2025, with the Kraków date sitting between Vienna on November 29 and Budapest on December 2, and Aesthetic Perfection opening. The concert recording that came out of it, “Live In Kraków”, arrives as a DVD, a Blu-ray, a CD and Blu-ray digipak, a limited KiT, a black double LP, a gold double cassette and a set of collector editions, including a 4,000-copy fan box. The full format rundown and setlist are in the Side-Line announcement linked above; the Blu-ray is region-free and carries a 16 age rating. Pre-orders run through the Out Of Line shop, and the two live singles are on the usual streaming services. About Till Lindemann Till Lindemann, born in Leipzig on January 4, 1963, has been the vocalist and lyricist of Rammstein since the band formed in Berlin in 1994. His work outside the group started with Lindemann, the duo with Swedish producer Peter Tägtgren that released “Skills in Pills” on Warner in 2015 and “F & M” on Universal on November 22, 2019. Tägtgren left in November 2020. Lindemann continued under his own name with the single “Ich hasse Kinder” on May 31, 2021 and the self-released album “Zunge” on November 3, 2023, which he toured across Europe that November and December. Till Lindemann signed to Out Of Line in early 2025. The “Meine Welt” EP came out digitally on December 20, 2024 and physically on March 28, 2025, with CD remixes by Aesthetic Perfection and by Megabot featuring Zacky Vengeance of Avenged Sevenfold. A Hocico remix of “Und die Engel singen” followed in July 2025, and “Es brennt…” in March 2026, with alternate versions by Alex Terrible of Slaughter To Prevail and Greg Mackintosh of Paradise Lost. The “Meine Welt” tour took that material into arenas across 2025 and 2026, and the first edition of TILL FEST took place in Leipzig in 2025. “Du hast kein Herz (Live In Kraków)” is the second extract from the concert recording that closes that tour cycle on record, and the first Till Lindemann live album under his own name.

items.body: For this new EP, Serbian producer Goran Alavux has teamed up with the Dutch label New York Haunted. It features four tracks that quickly immerse the listener in Alavux’s brand of Dark-Techno. Two of the tracks are hard and dark, at times interwoven with Industrial sounds and occasionally infused with a touch of EBM. In my opinion, these are the stronger tracks. The other two tracks don’t sound bad, but they are a bit too repetitive for my taste and lack the same menacing quality. Alavux always has something to offer, consistently combining high productivity with quality. (Rating:7). Listen to “M 5.3”: NYH404 03 Alavux – M 5.3. by New York Haunted About Alavux Alavux is the main recording alias of Serbian producer Goran Alavuk, who also records as Solaris Path. Discogs lists his releases from 2008 onwards on labels including Twilight 76 Records, Vocode Records, Bass Agenda Recordings, Diffuse Reality, Bunker Records and his own 0ktag0n Records, where the “Underground Is Resistance” series appears. Side-Line reviewed Polar Light on Adriatiko Recordings in January 2026 and Underground Is Resistance on 0ktag0n Records in February 2026. “Illusions” was released by New York Haunted on 28 May 2026 as a download. The four tracks are “Illusions”, “Aerial”, “M 5.3.” and “Mutatio”. No production credits are listed on the Bandcamp page and the EP has no Discogs entry at the time of writing. It is the third Alavux release reviewed on Side-Line in 2026.

items.body: Every spectacle contains a private bargain with disaster. Fireworks make that bargain visible: powder and metal are prepared for beauty, ignited at close range, and trusted to travel in the promised direction. When the trajectory fails, celebration becomes panic before the eye can separate pleasure from fear. A relationship ruled by manipulation follows a similar course. Possession borrows the language of protection, dependency passes for devotion, and the danger becomes obvious only after the fuse has already burned its way down. Australian witch house and dream pop duo dusk2dawn place that collision at the center of It Kills Me Every Time. The downtempo lament is the second single from their debut album, Make A Wish, due September 11, 2026, through DERO Arcade. It follows Psalm 23, the record’s first official single, released in July. The recording opens in a distant hum that could be a roadway heard through concrete, then sinks into a deeper metallic drone. Synthesizers spread outward in broad, gauzy layers, carrying something of Blade Runner’s nocturnal grandeur through the haze of shoegaze and dreampop. A slow, shuffling drumbeat gives the track its narcotized gait. Jack Mannix sings with a dull, depleted sorrow, his voice seemingly drawn from a heart where hope has been reduced to residue. Finn Parker keeps widening the arrangement behind him, laying sheet after sheet of synth across the rhythm until the music reaches the desolate scale of The Cure’s slowest pieces on Disintegration and Wish. Written around manipulation, betrayal, boredom, possession, and dependency, It Kills Me Every Time dwells inside an attachment where harm has repeated so often that it begins to feel like the governing law. The measured tempo gives every phrase room to sink in, while the massed keyboards turn sorrow into something physical, pressing against the vocal from all sides. The accompanying video extends that condition into a catalogue of amateur fireworks disasters. Grainy found footage shows driveways, parking lots, wet plazas, and crowded public displays briefly transformed by fountains and rockets that veer sideways, topple, or burst at ground level. People scatter as white flashes burn out the camera sensor; cars and houses disappear behind red smoke; one doomed attempt gives way to another. Edited by Parker from clips sourced by Mannix, the film finds a grimly apt image for the song’s damaged intimacy: people remain close to something designed to explode because they still want the promised beauty. “We often work with found footage for our videos, previously we have used footage of an exotic dancer in a masonic lodge, or a montage of controlled building demolitions. I like the way that these visuals provide an emotional metaphor for the music and create a somewhat hypnotic and disturbing viewing experience, with the aesthetics of lost media and youtube rabbit holes. For this video the firework accident footage seemed fitting as it was this document of people creating these dangerous and beautiful displays of explosives, and an attempt at one thing that goes wrong and creates another. The lengths and risks people will endure for a spectacle” Watch the video for It Kills Me Every Time below: dusk2dawn brings Finn Parker of Eternal Dust together with Jack Mannix of Circle Pit. The two first met as teenagers within Sydney’s post-punk scene and briefly played in a band alongside future members of Low Life and Exek. Parker began dusk2dawn as a solo outlet for the witch house- and gabber-informed instrumentals he was making while active in Eternal Dust, inviting Mannix to join as vocalist and lyricist in late 2022. Early demos followed during a brief period when they shared an apartment in Kings Cross and were released through Mannix’s DERO Arcade. A handful of sold-out appearances in Sydney and Melbourne accompanied the pair’s work on what would become Make A Wish. Across the album, dusk2dawn move from the punk and industrial pressure of opening track Angel Face into dream pop and witch house ballads such as soul2keep, Heaven Is Only In Hell, and Gateway. Psalm 23, the title track, and Behind The Mask draw the record toward darker gothic forms. Its subjects remain equally severe, moving among suffering, grief, sublimation, transcendence, decay, mutation, and possession. Of his approach to the lyrics, Mannix says: “I try to make my lyrics for this project as obtuse and simple as possible, to create a screen that the listener can easily project their own experiences and interpretations onto. I want to cast a spell that is at once loaded and universal – the real meaning buried in the simplest possible terms.” Make A Wish was recorded and mixed by Finn Parker and Eduardo Bianchino, then mastered by Wayne Sunderland at Suture Mastering. The album arrives September 11 through DERO Arcade. Listen to It Kills Me Every Time below and pre-order the album here. Make A Wish by dusk2dawn Revisit Psalm 23, the first official single from Make A Wish, below: Watch the duo’s earlier videos below: soul2keep: Heaven Is Only In Hell: Follow dusk2dawn: Instagram YouTube Bandcamp The post When the Fireworks Fail — Australian Dream Pop Duo dusk2dawn Light the Fuse in Video for “It Kills Me Every Time” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: There is a considerable buzz around Showing Teeth with the project already collecting nearly a quarter of a million followers on Instagram. Throw in a recent cover interview with Kerrang! plus a support slot for Bring Me The Horizon at their huge show in Manchester's BEC arena, and it's fair to say expectations are high. The band is essentially a solo project (there is a band for live shows), with versatile singer/songwriter Addison being the sole creative mind behind everything on debut EP, A Fate Worse Than Loneliness.This may be Showing Teeth's debut EP, but the quality of production would tell you otherwise. Everything feels polished, driven and agonised over. However, as is often the case on debut releases, it is difficult to pin down a definitive sound, mainly due to the songwriting dipping toes into so many genres throughout the seven tracks on offer. Initially you're lured into thinking this is going to be a blast of frenetic death/metalcore, with opener “Bad Exchanges” blowing the doors clean off with its bludgeoning intensity. Think along the lines of Knocked Loose teaming up with Employed To Serve at their heaviest and you’re getting close. But, by the time you get to the soaring Ariana Grande-esque pop choruses on finale “Paradigm”, you might be a tad confused with what direction this project wants to go in.  Addison's vocal range is absolutely incredible and clearly the star of the show. Even before we get to the clean vocals her palette of screams are simply stunning. Whether it be guttural growls or high pitched rasps it's all delivered with energy and venom. I’m pleased the clean vocals are not implemented lavishly on every track, especially as there is so much variation in the screams. For example, there's plenty of spiky texture on “Labyrinth” without the, admittedly catchy as hell, angelic chorus. Djent-laden “Rip” uses them in a different way, with a fleeting cameo at the one minute mark, before returning for a suitably flourishing finale. “Make It Out” and “Shallow Grave” do feel like slight mis-steps and go too far down a predictable nu-metal path, but I’m sure I will be in the minority on this point as the more accessible vocals are definitely a huge part of the bands appeal. In fact, I’m going to completely contradict myself now, but I would have preferred “Paradigm” to be brave, ditch the screams entirely, and just embrace its pop anthem glory. It will be interesting to see which direction they decide to go in for their inevitable full length release, and I hope they manage to laser focus their sound while still holding on to the ferocity present on "Bad Exchanges". I have no doubt that Showing Teeth are going to blow up insanely big over the next 12-18 months and this can only be a good thing for extreme metal, especially if they act as a new gateway for kids to discover other heavy bands. That being said, this is an incredibly promising debut release showcasing a serious vocal talent that will likely be filling arenas in years to come.

items.body: The age-old adage: what do you get when Genesis's Steve Hackett and Marillion's Steve Rothery cross proggy paths? Hopefully you haven't been asking that question too long, since The Roaring Waves is the first instance of the duo collaborating studio-wise. Yes, Rothery joined Hackett during the latter's 2013 concert at the Hammersmith Odeon, but this marks the premiere point of studio cooperation. It's quite surprising that these two musicians, each with decades upon decades of expertise in adjacent fields, only released a project last Friday. Hackett's been silent since 2023's The Circus and the Nightwhale, and Rothery's last release, The Ghosts of Pripyat, is nine years Nightwhale's elder. Eight years in the making led up to this (which explains the dip in activity from the respective players), so it's about time some classic, guitar-driven prog came my way, and I'd never ignore an artistic couplet such as Hackett & Rothery, so follow me as we dive straight into The Roaring Waves. It comes as no surprise, considering the kith and kin that are two progressive rock guitarists, that the record is purely instrumental. Think of it comfortably, rather than a full-throttle, blistering shredfest akin to some breakaway Dream Theater endeavor. The Steves rely on textural atmospherics instead of masturbatory showiness to craft the record's concept: the "profundity of the sea". Don't bend your legs and widen your feet just yet–the two artists bring the ocean to you. Whether they do so through a steady rocking pattern or electronic-laden passages is up to the natural course of Mother Nature's vast waterscapes. While the idea is intriguing, Hackett and Rothery only periodically conjure the nautical imagery exhibited on the album's cover. While the masterful duo trade winding, melancholic notes over shifting drum patterns (see "Sandsend," "The Black Sea") or simple ambience ("K-129"), there aren't enough sonic tinges to communicate such an expansive, oceanic environment. Little nods, like the natural sound effects in the opening track "The Storm," or the electronic pitter-patter sprinkled throughout The Roaring Waves' bulk of songs, rein me in from deeming the LP a standard instrumental release.This brings up a talking point heavily debated within the rock and metal community. Are instrumental records boring? Intrinsically, they are, when considering the heaviness of the genre. Of course, ambient albums surely mustn't include lyrics, but should progressive rock? Plenty of classics, like Camel's The Snow Goose or Mike Oldfield's myriad of sprawling epics, benefit from the instrumental's activity. There's nothing stagnant about these examples, hence their cult fame. The Roaring Waves waits until the final song, "Pacific Coast Highway," to supply any rocking action, and even that doesn't honestly fit in with the sea-ness. The twangy rip from Hackett's harmonica and symphonic feel aren't choices I would've made to muster oceanic vibes, and for this excitement, I had to tread thirty-eight-or-so minutes of consoling yet unwavering waters. I didn't plunge to the depths of The Roaring Waves expecting a tsunami; more of a point break. Instead, my bark swayed gently, rendering the gumption I gathered unnecessary.They can play their water pans and layer keyboard upon synth, but I want more from these illustrious talents. Granted, I wasn't a huge fan of Marillion (or neo-prog, actually), and Genesis fell off for me, along with everyone else, when the 80s pop wave decimated prog. Hackett helped the band navigate some of the finest recordings of the 70s; however, he should've administered a larger dose of his vintage spirit with his guitarmate. Dexterously, this collaboration fell short, but if you need forty-five minutes of simple backing tunes, you'll find these waves better fit for your boat. The Roaring Waves (24-bit HD audio) by Steve Hackett, Steve Rothery

items.body: The Internet is undefeated when it comes to complaining. Even more so when it comes to something super important like… a stoner doom band putting out a new record without a foundational member. I kid a little bit, but in gathering the pulse of the doom community over the last few weeks, it’s clear the announcement of Sleep’s new lineup and singles are going over like a fart in church for many fans. I’m seeing everything from the silly and stubborn “No Pike, no Sleep” to extremely sophisticated barbs like “they should change the band name to Nap.” To be honest, I get why people are upset. Sleep has coughed up some of the very best the genre has to offer. I’ll argue that 2018’s The Sciences is the group’s crowning achievement, my default suggestion to anyone pursuing the genre, and an all-time personal favorite—all in no small part due to Matt Pike’s presence of magnificent riffitude and scuzzy guitar tone.No doubt shaking up the personnel in a three-piece is going to make a difference. Further souring the recent discourse is the “firing” of drummer Jason Roeder, now back in his rightful place with Neurosis. It’s apparent that Al Cisneros is calling the shots for Sleep, and while many have viewed this as some kind of power trip, I’d argue it would be far stranger to have an Al-less version of Sleep—or for him to start an entirely new band to play this style of music. The cynic in me says that if Hempispheres were released under a different name, the grumpiest of online grumps would dismiss it as “wannabe Sleep” or something. Whatever. Bands come and go, members change, and life goes on. There are multitudes of bands who’ve changed lineups and moved on from key members, and this is no different. Whatever idea one has about what this band is or should be isn’t tied to any single person, and I think that’s an important distinction to keep in mind when listening to this record.All that said, my outlook going into Hempispheres is probably sunnier than most. Enlisting former Shrinebuilder collaborator and Melvins sticksman legend Dale Crover is a wonderful, if not downright obvious choice. There’s history there, dude kicks like a mule, and he can groove with the best of ’em. On the other hand, filling Pike’s shoes with Bud Dupree (Void) is a surprising call. A speedy ’80s D.C. hardcore guitarist at the helm of the S.S. Slow & Low? Now this was certain to garner some attention, but I wasn’t clear on how this’d actually play out. Sure, Pike is no stranger to ferocity and speed, but this substitution on paper seemed like it could really shake things up. Does it?Well, the rollout for Hempispheres might have you thinking so. Lead single “Have Spacesuit Will Travel,” in particular the “(4:20 Flexi Edit),” is just about as boilerplate as Sleep can get. The production is more bass-forward, we get some sci-fi synths in the mix for a little character, but it’s a curious choice to introduce the new lineup—an (only) four-freakin-minute Sleep song? No substantial soloing? How can anyone couch-lock into something so brief? It all felt a little …off. Truth be told, this is corrected on the album cut—I knew there were some solos hiding from us—but I’m left wondering why the introduction to this new lineup was cut so short, literally. Oddly enough, the second single, “The Morrisist,” landed in the same fashion: another sub-five-minute, heavy-on-the-eerie-atmosphere diddy, replete with more cosmic synths and an Om-like meditative groove. Shortform Sleep, especially on the heels of the phenomenal and utterly indulgent forays of The Sciences, hinted at something else entirely: a dramatic change in direction. And yet, fortunately, that’s not the case.The title-track centerpiece wastes no time getting cooking with that crooked, lurching Sleep groove we all know and love. The creepy spacey synths return, just enough to lend some distinguishing presence (they pop up time and time again, and I kinda love it?), but more importantly, Dupree gets his chance to lend his own signature. I gotta say, I’m really feeling what this dude lays down, and I absolutely adore how you can hear his flavor come through in a format that actually gives him time to let loose. (Seriously, take 10 minutes and throw those Void EPs on to get a little micro-taste of what you’ll find here.) If he’s a chiller, more subdued player than Pike, he’s also a more patient and expressive one; there’s something weirdly dark and haunting about the tone he’s dialed in, and goddamn can he make that fucker scream when he climbs the fretboard. He meshes in nicely with the bass-forward production of Hempispheres. Where previous records had bass and guitar matching fire with fire, this record sounds more like IcyHot. Rest assured, the closing three minutes of those resin-coated leads in this title track are about as Sleep as it gets without being that Sleep: something to groove with, but more importantly, something worth getting lost in.This spirit continues throughout the remainder of the album. The groove again leads the way in the jammy “Arrival of the Industry Ships,” an eleven-minute whopper with this progressively deteriorating, blown-out bass that’s equal parts percussive and “holy shit” levels of fuckery at an appropriate high volume. Al and Bubba flex a bit on the jams here, something I hope is a peek at what to expect on the road (or maybe I’m just buzzin’ on the whole jam thing after seeing King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard cut loose at Field of Vision). Similarly, closer “Whole Wheat Mountain / Well Baked” instantly locks in on another ear-turning groove. Crover, like Roeder and others before him, balancing restraint and style, every fill matching pace and power. The riffing here is something old Sleep might’ve had a lil’ more oomph behind, and it’s one of the few times it feels like the production isn’t doing the song justice. And yet, when Dupree cuts in with a lead, it all seems to make more sense. The contrast in the guitars is super effective and, in a way, unlocks the angle they take on Hempispheres.This is a (more) groove-forward version of Sleep. I’ll admit, the riffs aren’t quite as delicious as they’ve been in the past, but these grooves fucking stick. Is it the best Sleep album, or, to ask another way, did you really think they’d ever top The Sciences? No. Is it still worth splurging on all the Indica you can get your mitts on for this record? Absofuckinglutely. So let’s hit the cliché buttons: first impressions aren’t everything, and expectation is the thief of joy. For real, give this one some time to sink in if your precious ears can handle the tonal shift. It’s apparent Bubba and Dale understand the assignment: this is unequivocally a Sleep record, but with a different atmosphere, a new planet to explore, if you will.. Ultimately, it’s the same Sleep, just a different strain. Hempispheres by Sleep Hemispheres is available digitally everywhere on September 3 via Third Man Records. (Strange there’s no vinyl, eh?) The comic book is also available for preorder via Third Man, due out September 22.

items.body: 会期：2026/06/12〜2026/06/17 アトリエ春風舎［東京都］ 作：山本正典 演出：山本正典＋原竹志 公式サイト：https://kotorikaigi.yangotonaki.com/2026/Gesuitou/ 『おかえりなさせませんなさい』が2025年の第69回岸田國士戯曲賞最終候補作にノミネートされ注目を集めたコトリ会議／山本正典。同作は第3回関西えんげき大賞で最優秀作品賞と観客投票ベストワン賞を受賞するなど高い評価を受け、劇団の代表作となった。そのコトリ会議の新作『この上のない下水筒』（作：山本正典、演出：山本正典＋原竹志）はしかし、これまでの作風の延長線上にありながら、劇団の新境地を示す作品となっている。 ある夜。東日出中ゴミ拾い部の元部員・朝倉くんの死を知った同じく元部員たちが彼の住んでいたアパートにやってくる。部員たちが顔を合わせるのは中学卒業以来28年ぶりのことだ。ゴミ拾い部の元部長で、ことあるごとに朝倉くんと対立していた木戸（阪本麻紀）、朝倉と親しくしながら、卒業後はゴミ拾い部のことを忘れたいと願い生きてきた磯部（のたにかな子）、いつも人の話を聞いていない朝倉派の尾田（原竹志）、そして朝倉派から部長派に寝返った小間井（花屋敷鴨）。ゴミ拾い部は何かしらの事件をきっかけに卒業を待たずして解散してしまったらしく、どうやら部員たちの間には、未だにそのことに起因するわだかまりがあるようだ。不在の朝倉を中心に久しぶりに再会した4人は思い出話を交わし互いの近況を尋ね合うが、ぎこちない会話はそこに強い不信が忍び込んでいるがゆえだろう。互いの不信が高まりゆくなか、やがて誰が置いたかわからない300万円が見つかって──。 ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ コトリ会議の作品はそのほぼすべての作品においてSF的な設定が導入されている。SFといってもその多くはハードなそれではなく、例えばほとんど脈絡なく思えるようなかたちで宇宙人や人間ではない登場人物が登場するような世界を舞台とする、SF風味とでも言うべきテイストのものだ。このSF的な設定はとぼけたセリフ回しと相まって、コトリ会議の「少し不思議」な唯一無二の世界観を作り上げている。『この上のない下水筒』も例外ではない。 実はこの作品にはもうひとりの登場人物がいる。不在の（遺体となって奥の部屋に安置されている）朝倉の部屋に置かれている仮の朝倉（山本正典）である。「安村先生が楽天で取り寄せ」て「いろいろあったから」と部員たちのために置いたのだというその仮の朝倉はしかし、本物とは「顔が全然違う」らしく、のっけから尾田に「もう少し本人に寄せようと思わなかったのかい」「顔だけでも似せないとただのおじさんじゃないか」と言われてしまう。セリフ回しともどもいかにもコトリ会議な展開である。 ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ さて、仮の朝倉は幽霊かクローンか、あるいはアンドロイドだろうかなどと思いながら観ていると、意外にも（？）仮の朝倉はこの作品の主題らしきものを体現する存在であることがわかってくる（いや結局のところアンドロイド（？）でもあるようなのだが……）。仮の朝倉が本物に似ていないという指摘はそのまま、28年ぶりに顔を見たのに棺の中にいるのが本物の朝倉だとどうして言えるのか、そもそも28年ぶりに会ったお互いが本人だとどうやってわかるのかという問いへと展開し、誰かの「本当の姿」を知ることなどできはしないのだという真理へと至るだろう。思いや思い出はすれ違い、それぞれが抱く人物像が「本人」と完全に一致することは決してない。たとえ朝倉が生きていたとして、周囲の人間が見ているのはどこまでいっても「仮の朝倉」でしかないのだ。 ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ 少しずつ各自の事情や思いが明らかになっていくワンシチュエーションの一幕劇は、ホラーの雰囲気をまとったサスペンスとして展開し、そして現実へと着地する。くすりと笑ってしまうような「少し不思議」な設定をそのまま、私たちが対峙する現実、あるいは他者という「謎」を体現するものとして提示してみせた山本の筆は、これまでの作品で「少し不思議」な世界を立ち上げてきたそれともまた違った巧みさを見せていた。少し不思議な世界を立ち上げることに留まらないその筆の力を改めて示してみせたのだと言ってもいい。「現実」を描くには山本の筆のナイーブさは危うくもあるものの（例えば本作で木戸に対して尾田が放つ「きみが性転換手術を施した朝倉くんなんじゃないのか」というセリフはまったく許容できるものではない。現在は性転換手術という言葉ではなく性別移行手術という言葉が使われているし、そもそもトランスジェンダーを取り巻く現在の状況を考えれば面白おかしく使っていい言葉でないことは自明だろう）、コトリ会議／山本正典の描く物語のさらなる広がりに期待したい。 『この上のない下水筒』ではコトリ会議としては2022年の『全部あったかいものは』以来の東京公演が実現したが、次は早くも10月に吉祥寺シアターで行なわれるショーケース公演『ラブ・演劇博 ─こちらの演劇、とおくのまちから。─』への参加が決定している。「地方を拠点に活動する劇団を吉祥寺シアターに招き、ショーケース形式で上演を行う」この企画では兵庫拠点のコトリ会議に加えて宮城のMICHInoX、岩手の冷蔵庫ポルカの作品も上演される予定だ。 観賞日：2026/06/17（水） 関連記事 コトリ会議『おみかんの明かり』（芸劇eyes番外編vol.3.『もしもしこちら弱いい派 ─かそけき声を聴くために─』）｜山﨑健太：artscapeレビュー（2021年08月01日号） コトリ会議『しずかミラクル』｜山﨑健太：artscapeレビュー（2018年07月01日号）

items.artist: B:A:N:S Band (Sophie Agnel/John Butcher/Pascal Niggenkemper/Ståle Liavik Solberg)
items.excerpt: Of the many things that make albums featuring John Butcher unique, I believe the most outstanding characteristic is not that he likes to play at unusual venues (caves, water reservoirs, oil tanks…), but rather the fact that every ensemble he plays with is so diverse and incomparable that it allows the listener to hear many different facets of his playing. items.body: Of the many things that make albums featuring John Butcher unique, I believe the most outstanding characteristic is not that he likes to play at unusual venues (caves, water reservoirs, oil tanks…), but rather the fact that every ensemble he plays with is so diverse and incomparable that it allows the listener to hear many different facets of his playing. In an interview with Brad Rose, Butcher said that when improvising, he likes to hear the musician behind the instrument, though it’s not important to him to hear the musicians putting themselves in the spotlight - on the contrary, he tends to seek subtlety. In general, he looks for musicians who have already developed a personal musical style and their own way of playing - something that truly feels like their own. It is therefore almost inevitable that the various ensembles he selects based on these criteria will possess a unique dynamic and sonic world. One of last year’s best albums was RARE , John Butcher’s duo with French pianist Sophie Agnel, with whom he had been playing quite frequently over the last few years. I especially liked their improvisational rigor and the relaxed, varied, and aleatoric moments. On RARE , I considered the pauses in the music to be the central element; on foams & mesh , it’s different, mainly due to Pascal Niggenkemper (bass) and Ståle Liavik Solberg (drums), because the two of them fill those gaps. Solberg, with whom Butcher has played since 2015 in many kinds of combinations, permeates the improvisation with his bone-dry and at times almost esoteric style, for example when he uses extended materials (especially in the quiet passages of the first track). This is complemented by Agnel’s trills, which she plays from inside the piano. Butcher contributes very delicate bird calls here, while Niggenkemper subtly saws at the very low strings of his bass. It feels as though one is listening to the goings-on in the courtyard of a Tibetan monastery. This can be heard around the 20-mark of the first, significantly longer improvisation on foam & mesh. Such passages contrast with highly expressive moments, in which the rhythm section performs in a demanding and driving manner, but Butcher remains unflappable and employs his entire repertoire - guttural sounds, chirps, tremolos, circular breathing, serial/repetitive patterns, etc. - with casual ease. Only at the end of the track Agnel’s clusters and crescendos, Niggenkemper’s alienated drones and Solberg’s accentuated interceptions tempt him into vibrato-heavy phrases. The album was recorded at the artacts festival in St. Johann/Austria in 2024 and in the first part of the encore the musicians showcase extended playing techniques, with Niggenkemper and Agnel holding the improvisation together by a somber drone. Then the bass and piano shift imperceptibly into their normal registers, and the piece grows denser, builds in intensity, becoming louder and more concentrated - like a tornado - before dissolving perfectly. foam & mesh is an extraordinary album, the band is a superb match. They have played only three concerts so far and I think I’m not the only one who hopes that there will be more to come. foam & mesh is available as a CD and as a download. You can buy and listen to the album on the label’s website: https://sluchaj.bandcamp.com/album/foam-mesh foam & mesh by B:A:N:S BAND: Sophie Agnel / John Butcher / Pascal Niggenkemper / Ståle Liavik Solberg Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.artist: Geof Bradfield / Myra Melford / Ben Goldberg / Dana Hall
items.excerpt: Label: Calligram Records, 2026 Personnel - Geof Bradfield: tenor and soprano saxophone, bass clarinet; Ben Goldberg: clarinet, contra alto clarinet; Myra Melford: piano; Dana Hall: drums. items.body: Label: Calligram Records, 2026 Personnel - Geof Bradfield: tenor and soprano saxophone, bass clarinet; Ben Goldberg: clarinet, contra alto clarinet; Myra Melford: piano; Dana Hall: drums. What a wonderful time I had listening to this fantastic bass-less quartet, whose powerful avant-garde jazz captivates from start to finish. Recorded live at Chicago’s legendary Green Mill, Open or Close gathers compositions from all four members—saxophonist Geof Bradfield, clarinetist Ben Goldberg, pianist Myra Melford, and drummer Dana Hall—who, having crossed musical paths before in several contexts, make a remarkable debut as a group here. Ornette Coleman’s “ Open or Close ” is the stunning opener, showcasing a memorable eight-note riff that gradually evolves into staccato activity resembling rhythmic shocks of vibrant color. Initially, Melford constructs melodies around that riff, with Hall’s percussive driving force as her sole support. Goldberg’s sinewy clarinet phrasing also prompts quick responses from the drummer and effective comping from Melford; then Bradfield offers an earthy, motivic solo packed with tension and release before the theme returns. Melford’s “ A Line With a Mind of Its Own ”, inspired by American painter and sculptor Cy Twombly, is built over an exquisite scale, patiently expressed as a chamber-jazz concerto with moderate snare-drum effervescence, accelerations, and mounting intensity. The pianist also contributes the adventurous “ The Kitchen ”. Goldberg also brings two contrasting yet extremely effective compositions: “ Study of the Blues ” is definitely not your standard model within the genre, but rather a slightly dissonant exploratory piece with a lot of interesting things going on; “ Three Ingredients ”, on the other hand, is a bop-inflected piece centered on an expeditious figure. Starting as a conversation between contra-alto and bass clarinets, the tune evolves into a sort of avant-garde ragtime. The groove-forward standouts are marvelous to witness, and they provide a setting in which each musician’s distinct personality emerges naturally. Bradfield’s “ No Brand ”, a dedication to South African pianist Abdullah Ibrahim, flows with a feel-good, six-beat contra-alto clarinet groove, hi-hat buoyancy, and melodic discernment fueled by the parallel motion created by soprano sax and piano. During Goldberg’s beautifully articulated statement, there is no disruption to the groove in the lower register as he and the pianist switch roles. By the end, Bradfield and Melford mirror each other in thrilling interplay. Another dedication to a South African musician, bassist Johnny Dyani, comes with “ Lonely Flowers ”, a piece Dyani wrote himself and first recorded in 1978. These African scents also bring a touch of Sun Ra’s exoticism into play, and I love Bradfield’s fierce improvisational spirit here on tenor. Brimming with creative ideas, Open or Close has no weak tracks, with each one evoking thoughtful moods and sonic stimulation. These four musicians reveal exceptional musical capabilities, and their collective effort comes highly recommended. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Open or Close ► 03 - No Brand ► 04 - Study of the Blues ► 06 - Lonely Flowers

items.tags: クラシック 現代音楽 intoxicate 2026 August クラシック 現代音楽 # リイシュー クラシック 水野修孝
items.excerpt: 日本の前衛芸術の鬼才・水野修孝の電子音楽を集成したCDがリリースされた。中でも“怒りの日”と題されたコンクレート作品は〈この作品は大音量で再生しなければならない〉という作曲者自身の指示が残されていることで知られる。去る6月、私とスリーシェルズはこの作品を文字通り大音量で再生するリスニングイベントを開催。当日はタンノイで普段の約3倍、100dB近い爆音で再生した。それはまさに音の斬撃そのもの。音が波であることを改めて実感すると共に、この作品はイヤホン等で聴くものではなく、大きなスピーカーを通して全身で浴びるように体感してこそ真価を発揮するのだと確信した。

items.body:
Kiko Mizuhara has officially released her debut solo single, 'Feelin’ Wee', via Stones Throw. Produced by John Carroll Kirby, the funky and playful track marks the actor, model, and entrepreneur's first official music release.

The single follows Mizuhara’s 2025 cover of Haruomi Hosono’s 'Fuku Wa Uchi Oni Wa Soto', created alongside her sister Yuka and Kirby. Following the collaboration, Kirby encouraged Mizuhara to write her own lyrics and record original music.

“I think human beings are like diamonds. Depending on the angle, you see completely different sides,” Mizuhara shared. “Because I have so many different sides, expressing them through music felt like a really fun and liberating process.”

'Feelin’ Wee' arrives with a music video directed by Luke Casey, which places Mizuhara in a surreal moving set populated by dancers, snowcapped mountains, stars, planets, and other shifting props. Kirby also appears surrounded by keyboards, seemingly playing multiple instruments with the help of an extra pair of hands.

items.body:
Diplomacy got a musical encore in Bangkok this week.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong joined Thailand Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul for an impromptu performance during an official dinner at Government House on 2 September, following the 5th Thailand-Singapore Leaders’ Retreat.

With Wong on guitar and Anutin taking the microphone, the two leaders performed The Beatles' 'Let It Be' and Bob Dylan's 'Blowin’ in the Wind'. Videos from the evening showed the pair playing and singing together in a light-hearted close to the day's official engagements.

Meanwhile, in Bangkok, Thailand’s prime minister sang “Let It Be” and “Blowin’ in the Wind” as Singapore’s prime minister played guitar.#Thailand #Singapore pic.twitter.com/G85S7ZJhXh

— Thai Enquirer (@ThaiEnquirer) September 2, 2026

The dinner was hosted by Anutin and his wife in honour of Wong and his wife during the Singapore leader's official visit to Thailand.

The musical moment followed talks aimed at deepening relations between Thailand and Singapore, with both sides agreeing to strengthen cooperation across areas including energy and food security, the digital economy, defence, supply chains, and efforts to combat transnational crime.

Concluded my first Singapore-Thailand Leaders’ Retreat with PM Anutin. I deeply appreciate his friendship and warm hospitality. pic.twitter.com/SXtAcwzo3P

— Lawrence Wong (@LawrenceWongST) September 3, 2026

The meeting marked the first Thailand-Singapore Leaders’ Retreat in 11 years. The two countries also welcomed a joint statement outlining a forward-looking strategic partnership and discussed closer coordination ahead of Singapore and Thailand's respective ASEAN chairmanships.

For one evening, though, guitars and classic songs took centre stage — with two neighbouring prime ministers trading the conference room for a singalong.

Described as a mukbang anthem for food lovers, 'Yummy 88' celebrates food, indulgence, and good vibes. The single follows Lil Cherry & GOLDBUUDA’s viral 2020 track 'MUKKBANG!'.

Known for blending hip-hop, alternative pop, K-pop, electronic textures, and underground aesthetics, the duo have built a distinct identity through their experimental sound, visual style, and approach to storytelling.

Their Singapore appearance will be part of The Vibe Tribe, a recurring late-night event featuring high-energy DJ sets and guest performances. The night will also double as a birthday celebration for Singaporean hip-hop artist Shigga Shay.

Limp Bizkit, St. Vincent, Fontaines D.C. & More Announced For Lollapalooza India 2027

3 September 2026

Lollapalooza India has announced the line-up for its next edition, which takes place at Mumbai's Mahalaxmi Race Course on January 23-24, 2027.

The 2-day event will host British singer Olivia Dean, nu-metal band Limp Bizkit, pop group KATSEYE, Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C., Australian pop-rock band 5 Seconds of Summer, art-rock icon St. Vincent, Swedish House Mafia's Steve Angello and ¥ØU$UK€ ¥UK1MAT$U as some of the top draws this year. They'll be joined by UK singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri, Australian rock artist Ecca Vandal, US band Pinkshift, guitarist-producer Alain Johannes, Indonesian singer Isyana Sarasvati and Belgian duo 2manydjs, along with a one-off collaborative set from The Police's Stewart Copeland and composer Ricky Kej.

Homegrown talent on the lineup includes Aditya Gadhvi, Anuv Jain, Rajasthani folk theatrical production The Manganiyar Seduction, Zulan, Indian Ocean, BlackStratBlues, Kayan, Rhea Raj, Scribe, Maneesh On The Beat, RANJ x CLIFR, Swadesi, Yashraj, Varijashree Venugopal, Donn Bhat, Shanka Tribe, Rafiki, Curtain Blue, Run It's The Kid, Janisht Joshi, The Lightyears Explode, Meewakching, Calcutta Cowboy, Anoushka Maskey, Dohnraj & The Peculiars, Rasa, Noni-Mouse, Karshni, Raj and Shriya Rao.

For more information, follow Lollapalooza India.

items.body:
DMC World DJ Championships Return To India After 12 Years This Weekend

3 September 2026

After a 12-year hiatus, the DMC World DJ Championships are returning to India, with the national finals taking place at antiSOCIAL Mumbai on September 6.

Founded in 1985 as the Disco Mix Club, DMC is the longest-running global DJ competition, built around turntablism and the technical craft of DJing. Its championships have become a defining platform for scratch, beat juggling, cutting and other forms of turntable performance, with past winners including A-Trak, DJ Craze, DJ Kentaro, Q-Bert and Mixmaster Mike.

The India finals will feature two categories: the original DMC Classic Battle, which tests technical skill, creativity and musicality across a six-minute routine, and the Scratch Battle, dedicated entirely to scratch technique. Winners will earn the opportunity to represent India at the World Finals in London later this year.

The return of the competition and its culture in India is being led by DJ Uri alongside The Spindoctor, DJ Mocity and DJ Kan-i, with international champions DJ Fummy, Prime Cuts and Lobito Brigante appearing as judges and performers at the event. The day will also include workshops, equipment showcases and an afterparty.

items.body: Drone has an incredible tonal range. With sounds that range from calm to abrasive, drone can soothe or unsettle, like the distance between a refrigerator hum and an attack copter. These albums not only reflect the sounds that flow through our bodies, perceptible or not, but the hum, buzz and noise of everyday life. Earth’s empty aural spaces are being filled in slowly by sound, from subsonic frequency to passing plane. Those who work in this field underline the musical aspects of drone: subtle shifts, undulations, tension and release. Turning the intrusive into the sonically desired is yet another form of reclamation. Our cover image is from Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia‘s Phren on Maple Death, covered below. As always, our discussion of drone begins with the amazing Room40 label, whose roster focuses on drone yet is in no way restricted to it. We’ll be listing all of the imprint’s fall announcements here, including those of Someone Good, since Lawrence English has done such a fine job with advance publicity and it looks tidy! The first is a re-release of David Shea‘s I, originally on Sub Rosa; the Zorn-influenced album still sounds fresh and raucous (September 2). Next on the schedule is Werner Defeldecker + Eliad Wagner‘s Fray Field; readers may recall Dafeldecker’s Fathom Tidea with Lawrence English from earlier this year. This improvised album of double bass, synth and guitar is a whole different beast (September 11). Jannis Anastasakis and Peter Knight follow with Feather, a two-and-a-half-hour performance distilled to 32 minutes, light as air (September 18). The month ends with Hannes Strobl‘s Resonance IBK, an immersive five-part piece that blends field recordings of mountain and valley with complementary, drone-like music, and Prime Frequencies from mHz, who brought us 2024’s Material Prosody. The latter album, available in code and web-based formats, contains 47 investigations of sine waves and their relationship to prime numbers (September 25).   Room40’s October slate begins with Andrew Tuttle & Darren Cross‘ AT/DC (no, that’s not a typo)! This warm guitar and banjo set is enhanced by reverb and synthesizer, reminiscent of Rain Drinkers (October 2). Winter comes early with Philip Samartzis & Michael Vorfeld‘s Atmospheric Pressure, an acoustic reflection of a 36-hour Antarctic blizzard (October 9). Matt Rösner‘s Lost Meridians follows, described as “music to pause to,” reflecting the peace of open prairies and wide, unpolluted skies (October 16). Yann Novak‘s Discontinuity is a remixed response to Continuity, as well as a commentary on “deteriorating conditions in the U.S.” (October 16). Bruno Duplant investigates the nature of erosion through sound, offering l’usure du socle stable du monde, a two-part study meant to be experienced as a single piece (October 23). Steven Hess + Rutger Zuydervelt follow Re:collecting exactly a decade later with Re:construct. Times have changed, but there’s always a place for hope (October 30).   Maple Death continues its fabulous run with another box set produced in conjunction with Opale. Phren is a collaborative effort from Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia, introduced with an eleven-minute hymn that turns out to be the album’s most sedate selection, a worthy closer after the weight of the preceding tracks. The cover art is only the beginning; more of Sarah Mazzetti’s illustrations lie within (October 2). zakè‘s Tide Requiem for the Low Sea is a beauty to behold, available on increasingly rare picture disc vinyl. The music is like the end of summer, the art like an invitation to extend the season (September 2). The Sirens begins with the sound of an observatory door being opened. Geologist & Kyle Simon‘s music twinkles and shines, like a planetarium score or the biography of starlight (Outside Time, October 16). Calum Builder plays a reconstructed Copenhagen pipe organ on Although Changed, I Arise the Same, accompanied by vocal fragments culled from the Psalms. This results is a double reconstruction of faith and sound (thanatosis, September 25).   Tehran-born, Berlin-based Ava Rasti‘s No One Knows How Wild the Wind Blows is a harrowing reflection on current conditions in Iran. Aslan Mohammadpour‘s video for the title track starts as a benign home video before literally pulling back the curtain (FatCat / 130701, October 30). Falling into dark ambient-drone territory with titles such as “Circle of Black Candles,” Ajna‘s Mysterium Tremendum can’t wait for sunset. On this album, darkness is meant to evoke transcendence as well as fear (Winter-Light, September 4). Eric Angelo Bessel‘s Illusion of an Inland Ocean is murky, dark and mysterious, a reflection of everything from the ocean depths to the depths of the soul (Lore City Music, October 30). Seven bagpipe players and three basin players create an enveloping sound on Erwan Keravec‘s There will be no miracles here; check this video for insight on the performance. The organic sound borders on the otherworldly (Buda Musique, October 16). Rachel Shearer honors the earth and the Māori concept of whakapapa on Te Oro o Te Ao, as Maori vocals give way to a massive wall of field recordings and lead to a peaceful denouement (Thin Wrist Recordings, October 9). Falsetto singing, harmonium and cassette are the hallmarks of KKKAAARRREEENNNIIINNNAAA, an album as wild as its spelling bee title, courtesy of Charlemagne Palestine / Oren Ambarchi / Daniel O’Sullivan (Black Truffle, September 10).   Kai Niggemann‘s Climate and Violence began as music for the theatre performance “Denkraum der Utopien,” and has been updated and tweaked for this release. Since then, global climate change has only accelerated, and threatens to increase exponentially. The morphing music reflects shifts in atmospheric conditions and long-range forecasts (WAF80 Music, September 25). Giulio Aldinucci‘s Materia treats sound as matter that can be sculpted; the pieces feel like clay, molded and remolded, resisting their final forms (Karlrecords, September 18). Haarvöl‘s Overflowed Shelters is a direct commentary on recent events, highlighted by the harrowing first single, “Perpetual Ruins (a lament for Gaza).” The music reflects a slow-motion genocide, a horror from which many turn away, but that demands to be seen and confronted. There’s no escape in this music, nor should there be (Moving Furniture, September 26).   Thomas Brinkmann‘s GETGETGET is a single piece in two parts, born of a live performance. Listening is like traveling through the various permutations of drone, thin to thick, soft to loud, with percussion serving as additional texture (Editions Mego, October 23). A “diverse ecology of machines” is used on Ben Carey‘s INVENTIONS, which at times sounds like a cathedral tower and at other times a factory floor (Hospital Hill, September 14). Markus Solid creates immersive atmospheres by combining drone and electronics. Elastic Embrace is as mutable as its title, bent forward and back, refusing to break (Rhizome, September 25). ARROWOUNDS‘ Fludiic Time Cathedral is dark and mysterious, as one might expect from the artist who brought us In the Octopus Pond. The style is gothic rock drenched in shoegaze timbres, removed from the ether while still dripping, a worthy finale for Lost Tribe Sound’s Moss & Melee series (September 25). Richard Allen

items.body: For fans of CPU, Carl Finlow and electro’s wider continuum, IXRQ‘s command of the language will be immediately apparent. But this isn’t simply reverence for what has been. These are familiar components arranged with enough curiosity to remind us that electro’s future has never been about inventing the machine. It’s about continuing to find new things for it to say. Robotronic instruction sit beneath the surface Form & Fashion by IXRQ   A year after The Future Is Plastic, IXRQ returns to a form that has always understood the future as something assembled from memory. Electro is, after all, a genre built on recurring signals: machines imagining themselves as human, humans imagining themselves as machines, and a handful of sounds carrying decades of accumulated meaning. Across these four cuts, IXRQ works fluently within that vocabulary while resisting the temptation to simply reproduce it. The European lens is unmistakable. Rotherian propulsion and robotronic instruction sit beneath the surface, but the EP’s pleasures are found in its details: 808 patterns that groove rather than merely function, clipped Ensoniq fragments, synth probes disappearing into reverb, and pads that open up spaces where the rhythm can momentarily lose its certainty. Vocoders issue commands, naturally, but there is something pleasingly ambiguous about who exactly is listening. Creating tension between the archetypal and th​e individual :: That tension between the archetypal and th​e individual gives the EP its shape. “I Am Modeled” arrives with stoic authority, its clipped commands establishing an atmosphere of cool, programmed detachment, while “Signal Bridge” tightens the machinery into taut, economical funk, finding its momentum in crisp interplay between rhythm and circuitry. Personal favorite “Opal Tilt” pushes the established syntax further, its fat bass and subtly displaced ideas suggesting a system beginning to think beyond its programming, bending the familiar grammar into something altogether more playful and physical. Closer “XPVC Cascer,” meanwhile, alters the equation through pace alone, accelerating the final transmission into a more urgent, restless space. For fans of CPU, Carl Finlow and electro’s wider continuum, IXRQ‘s command of the language will be immediately apparent. But this isn’t simply reverence for what has been. These are familiar components arranged with enough curiosity to remind us that electro’s future has never been about inventing the machine. It’s about continuing to find new things for it to say. Form & Fashion is available on SEQ:RUN. [Bandcamp] Form & Fashion by IXRQThe post IXRQ :: Form & Fashion EP (SEQ:RUN) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Concept Record not only works as a creative tool; it demonstrates what can be created when Professor Ben’s instruction is heeded. The concept is to use this record alongside other records to make new records, while providing a legitimate D.H.S. album of its own right—one that embraces the features that help make physical records so fun and appealing. The record is the concept Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Ben Stokes is no stranger to concept albums. The albums he has released this century as Dimensional Holofonic Sound (D.H.S., to the initiated) and under the moniker Quietworld could all legitimately be labeled “concept records.” 2002’s Attention Earth People was an ode to ’50s and ’60s sci-fi and outer space. The “disturbing Muzak” of Quietworld’s Relaxalot was like walking through a Backrooms-style retro shopping mall—a boomer’s advertising fever dream. Then came D.H.S.’s 2020 music visualizer, Seeing Is Believing, with the vinyl edition even including a pair of classic red-and-blue glasses for watching the album’s videos online in 3D. Oh, let’s not forget his hand in the Tino’s Breaks series, led by an action figure who serves as an instructor in Latin beats. So it may seem a bit on the nose that D.H.S.’s new album is titled Concept Record—until you spend time with what Stokes has crafted here. After a couple of playthroughs, you realize the title could also be presented as “Concept: Record,” because on this album, the record is the concept. Fully realized jams :: Concept Record is a self-proclaimed “instrument disguised as an album,” according to Dimensional Holofonic Sound’s Bandcamp page, where you can currently pick up both digital and vinyl versions if you’re attentive and lucky enough. That description is certainly apt. Many of the tracks are ripe for a DJ’s arsenal, with loads of potential—and actual—loops throughout. Turntable DJs and creators are especially well equipped, as the double-vinyl version contains fifteen locked grooves with eternally repeating loops that stop only when you lift the needle. This isn’t merely a scratching record or DJ tool, though. While there are dedicated loop tracks and spoken vignettes, the majority of the album consists of fully realized jams. Many tracks begin stripped back or include sparser sections, seemingly designed to be sampled and looped into new creations, but D.H.S. expertly layers bouncing bass, bleeping synths, effects, and samples onto his beats, building them into genuinely danceable ravers. Stokes pulls out all his best tricks for this offering, treating us to a smorgasbord of what he’s learned over the last three decades. His ability to evoke nostalgic futurism through vintage dialogue and samples paired with modern electronic sounds is evident from the get-go in the arpeggiated title track, “Concept Record.” There’s the Quietworld-tinged “Hospital Tent,” the glitchy unease of “Chatter,” and the dark horror of “Chit Chat.” His prowess with cut-and-paste breakbeat rhythms is on full display in the Tino-esque “Maestro Music” and caffeinated “Takeoffthecoffeepotweputitdownupright,” and there’s bleep bliss found in the lead single “Supersonic Holofonic,” and cuts “Electro Pop” and “Concept Music,” the latter featuring Oakland musician Konceptualizer. Is that meta enough for you? Concept Record is another winning concept :: What shines brightest—and will have you throwing a personal mini-rave in your living room—is the acid, and D.H.S. serves up a potent dose. “Green Acid (Jack Dangers Remix)” is a clear standout, and having Dangers drop in is yet another brilliant treat from Stokes’ bag of tricks. The aforementioned “Supersonic Holofonic” is burbly enough to keep the trip going, blending into the electro-acid of “Cut To Black,” followed by the flashback of the buoyant “Full Blackout.” Now where did I put those glow sticks? In the end, Concept Record is another winning concept from Ben Stokes. He gives us the record as a musical tool, embodied in the vinyl’s locked-groove loops, and the record as a cohesive collection of songs. The LPs also serve as a unique listening experience, with a slightly altered track order, extra bits, and alternate versions/edits. (“Cut To Black” has a completely different vibe and mix on the vinyl.) Sides 1 and 3 even have zoetrope labels. You can only get that on a record. An electrified voice at the beginning of “Electro Pop”—at least on the digital version—sums up a core idea well, commanding the listener to “Do things… don’t fritter away your time… create, act… and be somebody.” Concept Record not only works as a creative tool; it demonstrates what can be created when Professor Ben’s instruction is heeded. The concept is to use this record alongside other records to make new records, while providing a legitimate D.H.S. album of its own right—one that embraces the features that help make physical records so fun and appealing. Concept Record succeeds on all counts. A+. Concept Record is available on Bandcamp. Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound  The post Dimensional Holofonic Sound :: Concept Record (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: There’s something particularly satisfying about hearing forgotten tracks recovered, revisited and finally released for others to discover. Off-Cuts (2014–2021) doesn’t feel like a scattered collection of archival material; instead, it comes across as a carefully gathered snapshot of a creative period, proving that these pieces still have plenty to say. Serving as a fine snapshot of the artist’s creative phase Off-Cuts (2014–2021) by Scarper   Steve Young (aka Scarper) continues to navigate a world of abstract electronics, consistently catching our attention through his output on his own Plexus imprint. Aptly titled Off-Cuts (2014–2021), this release brings together previously unreleased tracks from his Warmer Squares and E-Funk periods—pieces that might otherwise have remained buried within Young’s personal catalog, now recovered and given a new life. Serving as a fine snapshot of the artist’s creative phase across these seven years, all eight tracks have aged remarkably well, revealing qualities that feel less like forgotten leftovers and more like sounds waiting to be rediscovered. “Skynet (Dial-Up ’99 Mix)” immediately transports us back to the modem-era haze of the ’90s, cascading into an ambient swirl of sonic activity, soundtrack-like fragments and imploding, beat-driven beauty. “Rinse & Repeat (Head & Shoulders Mix)” ventures further into ambient techno territory, while the more upfront “Nightshift (Acid Tuesday Mix)” shuffles bass and percussion into a frenetic, dancefloor-ready rush. It’s within the (somewhat) slower pieces, though​, that Young really opens things up. The erratic, glitch-infested pulse of “Outlier (You’re My Skweeero Mix)” feels congested and fractured as it moves through downtempo breakbeat strains, while standout “Polarity (Curse These Metal Hands Mix)” dips into acidic waters with a full-throttle techno drive, its abstract substructures constantly shifting beneath the surface. Toward the tail end, the release takes a distinctive electro-infused turn. “Ponderosa (Grilled T-Bone Mix)” pushes Young’s sound into more elevated territory, while the crunchy drum’n’bass collision of “Steppe (Runty-Bunting Mix)” feels remarkably fresh, regardless of when it was originally created. Bringing things to a chilled-out close, “Halocline (Deep Water Mix)” bubbles to the surface through finely shaped micro-melodies and a deeply nostalgic flutter that feels capable of drifting on indefinitely. There’s something particularly satisfying about hearing forgotten tracks recovered, revisited and finally released for others to discover. Off-Cuts (2014–2021) doesn’t feel like a scattered collection of archival material; instead, it comes across as a carefully gathered snapshot of a creative period, proving that these pieces still have plenty to say.
